subpx workbench · Setup › 2 Preprocess

Preprocessing in the workbench

Preprocessing makes a second, cleaned copy of the page. The workbench keeps both copies side by side, each with its own holes, CD and pitch, and one switch decides which copy you look at and measure.

The bottom line: cleaner pixels are not better CDs

Measured on a synthetic page whose noise-free version is known (the example page, described below), half-area CD:

  • Wiener cuts the pixel noise from 7.2 to 2.4 grey levels, but hole-to-hole size differences come out at only 0.53 of their true size.
  • Mean hole, automatic K keeps only 20 % of a real 5 % CD step between two halves of the page.
  • Mean hole, K = 32 keeps the CD differences, but the CD scatter only drops from 0.187 to 0.171 px.

So a smaller CD spread after preprocessing can mean real differences were smoothed away. The test that decides it on real data: measure two exposures of the same holes. Preprocessing helps only if each hole's CD agrees better between the two exposures than it does raw.

Two versions of every page

The page you load is the raw page. Pressing Preprocess makes the preprocessed page from it with the method chosen in Setup. The raw page is never changed.

Each version has its own results drawer. The Preprocessed switch above the image (key P) picks the version on screen, and every run measures that version and fills its drawer. The other drawer keeps what it had.

What happens when you use it

  1. Pick a method in Setup › 2 Preprocess. Gaussian smoothing, Wiener filter or Mean hole, each with one or two numbers. A setting of 0 means Auto: the program picks the value from the page itself (below, for each method). The help line under the settings shows what each method did to CD on the synthetic test.
  2. Press Preprocess, or turn the switch on. The whole page is processed in the background, never just the analysis region: Wiener needs the whole page's pattern, and the mean hole learns from every hole on the page. The mean hole first finds the hole centres on the raw page with your Holes settings. When it is done, the switch turns on and the preprocessed page appears at the same contrast as the raw one. The log says what the method found, for example: Preprocessed page 0 (Wiener, noise auto) in 0.11 s: noise 7.2 grey levels (picked by Noise2Self); 9 % of the frequencies kept; removed 6.27 grey levels (sd). Preprocessed page 0 (mean hole, K auto) in 0.31 s: K = 3 (picked by Noise2Self), box radius 7 px; 2,709 of 2,709 holes rebuilt, 99 % of the page; removed 8.49 grey levels (sd) there.
  3. Preview holes, Measure CD or Measure pitch. With the switch on, these measure the preprocessed page and put their result in its drawer; the busy message reads "Measuring CD on the preprocessed page". The raw page's results are not touched.
  4. Press P to compare. Each version shows its own holes, CD and pitch. The comparison tools further down show both at once.

When you change a setting

The preprocessed page remembers the settings it was made with. Change any of them and only the preprocessed version goes out of date. The raw page's results never depend on Preprocess settings, so they stay up to date.

grey: not run green: up to date amber: changed since the result
Results are from earlier settings: preprocessing Gaussian 0.6 px -> Gaussian 1 pxRe-runRevert

What counts as a change

The method and its numbers. For the mean hole also the Holes settings it finds its centres with: pattern, threshold, dark holes, area min, area max and padding.

The two buttons

Re-run makes the preprocessed page again with the new settings and re-measures the result on screen, in one job. Revert puts the settings the result was made with back into Setup and leaves the results alone.

The example page

Every picture and number below comes from running the workbench's own preprocessing code on one synthetic page, made by scripts/preprocess_check.py. Because its noise-free version is known, we can see exactly what each method removed.

The page: 2,709 round holes on a square grid, 8.2 px apart (the spacing of the ACTIS test page), 4.8 px wide and blurred. Hole sizes vary 4 % from hole to hole, holes in the right half are 5 % larger, brightness flickers 10 % from hole to hole, and the pixel noise is 7.2 grey levels on an 8-bit scale where the holes peak near 190.

The three methods, on the pixels

All three turn the raw page into a preprocessed page of the same size. They differ in what they treat as noise.

Gaussian smoothing

setting: Sigma (px), default 0.6 · no Auto

Every pixel becomes a weighted average of itself and its neighbours. With sigma 0.6 px the pixel keeps 44 % of its own value and takes 11 % from each side neighbour and 3 % from each corner. The ring beyond adds 1 % in all.

The same fixed recipe on every page, so a brighter or dimmer page is treated alike. It also softens the hole edges, which is why it shows hole-shaped structure in the removed map further down.

Wiener filter

setting: Noise level (grey levels), 0 = Auto (Noise2Self)

A page of repeated holes is made of a few repeating patterns. Taken apart into its repeating patterns (its spectrum), the hole grid shows up as bright spots, and noise as a haze spread evenly everywhere. The filter keeps each pattern in proportion to how far it rises above the noise haze, and removes the haze.

How Auto picks the noise level. Noise2Self hides each pixel from the filter (its own share goes to its 8 neighbours) and predicts it from the rest. A real feature can be predicted from its neighbours; noise cannot. The program tries noise levels from 1 % of the page's spread up to all of it and keeps the one that predicts best.

On the example page it picked 7.20 grey levels; the true noise is 7.19. The log warns when the best value is at the end of the range tried. Noise shared along rows or columns makes it pick too little smoothing.

Mean hole

settings: Components K, Box radius (px); 0 = Auto

Cut a box around every hole (radius 7 px here: 3/4 of the hole spacing, rounded up). Fit each box's own brightness and background, so flicker does not count as a shape difference. Average all boxes, then find the few ways the boxes really differ from that average. Each box is rebuilt from the average plus its own amounts of the first K differences; everything else in the box is treated as noise.

≈ background + brightness × ( + a· + b· + c· )

How Auto picks K. The same hide-and-predict test: each pixel of each box is predicted from the rest of its box, for K = 0, 1, 2, … The K that predicts best wins: K = 3 on the example page (K = 2 on the real ACTIS test page).

The boxes overlap. Each pixel becomes a weighted mix of every box that covers it, with weight 1 at a box's centre falling to 0 at its edge. Pixels in no box stay raw. In the difference pictures, red adds light and blue takes it away (or the reverse, for a negative amount).

Checking it in the workbench

The workbench gives four places to compare the two versions without flipping back and forth:

Summary line

Above the image: the mean CD of the version on screen, with the other version's in brackets, e.g. "mean CD 4.471 px (raw page: 4.402)".

CD distribution

The other version's CDs drawn as a white outline on the same bins, with its count, mean and sd, and a reminder that a narrower histogram is precision only if the CDs still follow the true size one to one.

Hole inspector

An extra column "CD raw" or "CD pre": the same hole in the other version, matched by position (the hole whose cell holds the point, else the nearest within 3/4 of a pitch).

Show › Removed by preprocessing

Raw minus preprocessed over the whole page, red where preprocessing lowered a pixel and blue where it raised one. Hole-shaped structure means it changed the holes, not only the noise.

The Average hole tab

button: Average the holes · Grid: 1/4 px

This is not a preprocessing of the page. It stacks every hole of the result on screen at its own sub-pixel centre onto a grid 4 times finer than the pixels, on the raw page and on the preprocessed page with the same centres, and draws the x and y profiles with their width at half height. Brightness flicker is fitted out first. It shows the hole shape far more sharply than any single hole.

Fine print

  • Other pages turn on by themselves. With the switch on, showing another page makes that page's preprocessed version at once, with the current settings. Until it is ready the raw page is shown with the note "Raw page shown: this page is not preprocessed yet."
  • What always stays raw: the other pages of a vertically stacked view, and Align.
  • Flipping during a run. A result lands in the version it was started on, even if you flip the switch while it runs; the log says so.
  • Memory. Both versions of the open page are kept, plus the most recent other pages up to 3 pages and 3 GB in all; older pages' results are dropped with a log line.
  • Export adds preprocessed_image.npy (the whole page, float32), preprocess_meta.npz (the Auto curves and each hole's fitted brightness) and the settings in source.json.
  • Same functions outside the workbench: smooth_gaussian, denoise_wiener, denoise_mean_hole and average_hole in subpx.preprocess (see docs/preprocess.md).
